title: Delhi High Court: Paying Pagdi Cannot Shield A Tenant From Eviction For Bona Fide Need
seo_title: Delhi HC: Pagdi Can't Block Bona Fide Eviction
meta_description: Delhi HC: a tenant's 1988 pagdi payment cannot defeat a bona fide eviction, since the Rent Control Act bars pagdi payments outright.
case_name: Md. Kamruddin v. Devi Dayal Saini
body: Old Delhi and its neighbouring markets are full of tenancies that trace back decades, and a good many of them carry an unwritten extra payment on top of rent: pagdi, a lump sum handed over at the start of the tenancy that lowers the monthly rent a landlord can charge. Md. Kamruddin says he paid Rs. 65,000 in pagdi back in February 1988 when he took a ground-floor shop at 272/A, Masjid Moth, near Udai Park, to run his mechanic's workshop. That claim, and whether it could save him from an eviction order, is what the Delhi High Court weighed in a judgment dated 3 November 2026.

The landlord, Devi Dayal Saini, had moved the Rent Controller seeking Kamruddin's eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, on the ground that he needed the shop for his granddaughter, a practising advocate who wanted to set up her own office and had no other suitable space. The Senior Civil Judge-cum-Rent Controller at Saket found the landlord-tenant relationship undisputed, held the bona fide requirement established, and ruled that no reasonably suitable alternative accommodation was available to the landlord. On 16 May 2025 the Rent Controller dismissed Kamruddin's application for leave to defend and passed an eviction order against him.

Kamruddin took the matter to the High Court by way of revision under Section 25-B(8) of the Rent Control Act read with Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. His case had two limbs. First, he said Saini had other space to offer his granddaughter: the rear portion of the same ground floor, the first and second floors of the same building at 272/A, Masjid Moth, and a further property at 272, Masjid Moth in the same locality, four premises in all besides the one he occupied. Second, he revived the pagdi plea, adding that Saini had allegedly acknowledged the Rs. 65,000 payment at a meeting at his residence in March 2024, a conversation Kamruddin says he recorded and placed before the Rent Controller.

Before getting to either argument, Justice Harish Vaidyanathan Shankar had to deal with a procedural wrinkle. An earlier order in the same petition, passed in October 2025, had limited notice to the narrow question of how much time Kamruddin would need to vacate, after the court had already heard arguments on merits and found them unconvincing. When a new set of lawyers came on record for Kamruddin and tried to reopen the merits regardless, the court made its disapproval plain, noting that changing counsel does not wipe clean what has already been argued and decided. It heard the case afresh anyway, solely so that Kamruddin could have no grievance of not being heard, while making clear this was not to be read as approval of the tactic.

On the alternative accommodation point, the court found nothing wrong with the Rent Controller's reasoning. The disputed shop sits on the ground floor with direct access from the main road, while the spaces Kamruddin pointed to are either at the rear or on upper floors, locations a lawyer's office open to walk-in clients would manage far less well. Citing the Supreme Court's line of authority starting with Sarla Ahuja v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. and continued in Abid-Ul-Islam v. Inder Sain Dua, the bench repeated the settled position that a landlord, not his tenant, gets to decide which of his properties best answers his own need, and that a tenant cannot insist the landlord evict some other occupant instead.

The pagdi argument fared no better, and for a sharper reason than mere factual weakness. Even taking Kamruddin's version at its highest, the court said, the alleged payment would only explain why his rent was fixed at Rs. 400 a month rather than Rs. 1,141; it would not touch the admitted landlord-tenant relationship, the bona fide need, or the absence of suitable alternatives. Beyond that, Section 5(2)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act bars any person from charging or taking a premium or pagdi over and above rent in exchange for granting, renewing or continuing a tenancy. A payment the statute itself outlaws cannot be the foundation for resisting an eviction sought on an entirely separate, lawful ground, and the court held that the plea raised no triable issue at all.

Running through the whole judgment is a reminder of how narrow the High Court's revisional jurisdiction under the rent law actually is. The proviso to Section 25-B(8) gives it supervisory power over the Rent Controller's decision-making, not an appellate licence to reweigh the evidence and arrive at a different finding; interference is reserved for jurisdictional error, manifest illegality or a plea left wholly unconsidered. Finding none of that here, the court dismissed the revision petition as without merit, leaving the eviction order intact. For landlords and tenants sitting on old pagdi arrangements across Delhi's shop and market tenancies, many of which go back to the 1980s and 1990s on exactly this kind of informal premium, the ruling signals that the payment offers no shield once a genuine ground for eviction is made out.
why_it_matters: This ruling matters for Delhi's older shop and market tenancies, where informal pagdi payments remain common decades after they were first outlawed. It confirms that even a documented, acknowledged pagdi payment cannot block an eviction sought on genuine bona fide need, because the Rent Control Act itself treats the payment as illegal. It also reaffirms that a tenant cannot dictate which of a landlord's several properties should satisfy that need. Landlords pursuing eviction on bona fide grounds, and tenants weighing a leave-to-defend application, should treat pagdi arguments as largely irrelevant to resisting an otherwise well-founded eviction petition.
card_summary: Delhi HC: a tenant's claim of a 1988 pagdi payment cannot defeat a landlord's eviction of a Masjid Moth shop for bona fide need, since the Rent Control Act itself bars pagdi payments outright.
card_tip: An unlawful pagdi payment is not a defence to a bona fide eviction claim, and a tenant cannot insist the landlord vacate some other property instead of the one actually in dispute.
